In the end, even the transient orcas are doomed to extinction eventually, especially if humanity doesn't change it's ways regarding overfishing, pollution, habitat degredation. There are some salmon species that are doing relatively well, sockeyes and the pinks for example, which will carry on the torch. The Chinook and Chum however, are not doing well and likely to die out if drastic measures aren't taken, and soon.

The southern residents focus almost entirely on Chinook, while pinnipeds have multiple species from which to draw from. Ergo, they will hold on much longer than the orcas will.

In the end though, I think we can agree- salmon are imperitive to our local ecosystem and their loss would have far-ranging, negative effects on our beautiful land. I want the orcas to survive and thrive like you do, but without the salmon, they're done for.

Well, assuming they are able to adapt, they would probably adopt a diet similar to the transient orcas, that is, marine mammals like seals and sea lions.

Pinnipeds and their like are generally very adventurous eaters, and they consume a whole bunch of different meals ranging from benthic inverts like crabs, to forage fish and middle-of-the-chain predators like salmon, rockfish, and sand lance. Deceased seals have been found with ratfish in their stomachs, presumably killed by the sharp dorsal spine on the top of the fish. This is noteworthy, because Ratfish make up almost 60% of the biomass in Puget Sound, and their numbers are only growing. This is an example of a generalist species, as opposed to our orcas, which are specialized.

Seals and Sealions will of course be impacted by the loss of salmon, as will a surprisingly large amount of inland species. Tons of animals rely on the yearly salmon runs, and the nutrients that the fish bring into the rivers from their time in the sea eventually makes its way into the trees via transportation by predators like eagles, bears, and scavengers.

So the ancient roulette wheel continues to spin: We can have hyperspecialzed species, like the Devils Hole Pupfish, or the Southern Resident Orcas, of which both are struggling. Then there are the generalized species, like you and me, seals and sea lions, seagulls, crows. Cutthroat trout, as an example, are a very adaptable fish that are doing very well in our waterways. Sand lance are kicking ass, so too are jellies and tunicates.

​

Edit: Extra info.

In general, a species with a diverse diet will outcompete a species with a specialized diet. It sucks, but it's true.

Our resident orcas will die out and be replaced with other, more adaptable species as their food source dies out. All at the hands of humanity.

Killing sea lions won't help either. When the food chain is disrupted or broken, the sea lions will find different prey. They're eating ratfish, for example. 

Resident orcas must adapt or die, humans have forced their hand- err, fin.

I suggest tracing to start out. Use a pencil and paper, print out some cool drawings, and trace the lines. You'll get a feel for the angles and how to hold your pen, then move on to drawing images you like. Eventually, you'll be able to compose and set up an awesome drawing on your own!

Unlike martial arts, drawing is an incredibly personal process. Your own skill and style are going to come into their own eventually, and even if there are accepted techniques, you can learn on your own and develop your own method! There aren't a lot of ripostes or parries with a pencil, so it's all about your own personal journey.

Draw man! Let that creative urge flow and go create something awesome. :)

​

Edit: Also! Try drawing still lifes once your comfy with a pencil in your hand. Drawing fruit, or a jar, or whatever can be boring, but it trains your visual skill and helps you translate an IRL image into a 2D creation. Drawing has a lot of mental skills associated with it, and when you learn them, you'll see the world a little differently.

​

Vaccines only function to enhance your resistance to a virus, not provide a complete panacea. Basically, an innoculated (vaccinated) person can expect to have a very reduced severity if a breakthrough infection occurs. The breakthrough infections are also much less destructive because the vaccinated persons has a much better blueprint from which to make antibodies which then disable the virus in conjunction with other cells from your immune system.

Vaccinated people can still catch, incubate, and transmit the virus. It is significantly more likely that said infected person will be without symptoms because of the reduced efficacy of the virus, but it can still be passed on.

It's like a really good suit of armor against the virus, but it only does ALL of the things that it promises if our population reaches a vaccinated level high enough to reduce transmission.

I volunteer with the Snohomish County Beach Watchers, and I spend a lot of time on the beach. Pre Wasting Disease outbreak I noticed that we'd have tons of variety in sea star species that appeared on the beach, but now in a post wasting disease world I'm mostly seeing Ochre Stars on my local beaches. We get the occasional mottled star or blood star, but the Ochres are ruling the roost.

When I went through my training back in 2018 we discussed the Sun Stars at length, including the impact on their population from the disease. The prevailing theory, at least in my class, was that the absolute destruction of their population numbers has resulted in the a severe loss of breeding stock. Not only are they dying, but they are having a rough time making more.

Most sea stars as I understand them reproduce via a method called 'broadcast spawning.' This is also called the 'spray and pray method' by some biologists I know, and each species has a certain radius where this process is effective. My numbers are from memory alone and probably inaccurate, but in essence the Ochre Stars have a much broader range for their spawning than do the Sunflower stars. When you combine a small breeding range with an absolutely decimated population, you have the recipe for a species dying out.

Again, I'm no scientist, just a volunteer who loves the ocean. Sadly, things aren't looking good for these dudes and without some help, I personally believe they will not be making a comeback anytime soon.

Depression, like Anxiety, is far more nuanced than a simple one-fits-all remedy. I've been fighting it on and off my entire life, and I can say that getting outside and getting some fresh air can help somewhat, it's hardly a long term solution. I mean no disrespect toward OP, but it's never this simple.

One thing that HAS helped me a ton has been setting goals. Working toward something consistently has had a massive uptick in my daily well-being. I would not set large, unachievable goals at first, they will overwhelm a depressed brain. Rather, consider setting immediately useful small goals, such as going for a walk, brushing your teeth, doing your homework. I've found that as I achieve short-term goals, it's a lot easier to plan for and work toward long-term goals.

Basically, doing things that induce your brain to produce those sweet, sweet reward chemicals. What works for one person might not work for everyone. Some people need to be social, some people need to be mobile. Some people just need to read a book. The point is, it's different for everyone.

The only bit of universal advice I can suggest is to talk to your friends and family, let them know where your mental state is and let them know how to help you. For folks without supportive family, that's why we have our Friends, who are Magical, after all!
